1:
Ellicott sets the scene, the parting from Laban having fallen on the line dividing Aramean from Canaanite ground, where Laban could find no allies, so that Jacob now travels through the country promised to his seed with Esau before him. Henry marks the same relief, and draws the lesson that when God has helped us through one difficulty we should go on the more cheerfully. Calvin puts it more darkly, that Jacob proceeds in trepidation as one going to the slaughter, the brother's cruelty being as much to be feared as the father-in-law's, and that the Lord affords timely succour to a man who might otherwise sink. Both find the timing instructive, the comfort coming in a calm interval rather than amid the agitation, because God will have us provide for trouble while at peace and afterwards live upon former experiences.

Calvin assigns the vision a twofold use, to remove the cause of terror before the trial and to fix the memory of the deliverance already given, since scarcely one man in a hundred lifts his eyes to heaven while God is helping him. Gill takes the appearance to have been human, in the habit and accoutrements of soldiers, which is why they are afterwards called a host, and reports Aben Ezra's opinion that Jacob alone saw them, as Elisha saw before his servant. Henry and Wesley leave open whether it was a vision by day or a dream by night, as when he saw the angels on the ladder. Ellicott collects the attempts to reduce the vision, that the messengers were prophets, a caravan bringing news of Esau in Seir, or a company sent by Rebekah, and prefers a dream answering to the earlier vision of the stairs.

Clarke turns aside to the word itself, from a Greek noun meaning messenger, rendered in the old English Bibles a tidings-bringer, and a Hebrew root meaning to send. He quotes Augustine that it is a name not of nature but of office, which is why the same word serves for a human envoy, a prophet, a priest and a celestial spirit, and Parkhurst that the angel of Jehovah is God's means of becoming visible. On Mahanaim, Clarke takes the two camps to be the angels and Jacob's own company, or else reads the word as a plural, and notes that a city was afterwards built there and given to the priests. Ellicott allows both readings, Jacob's camp with the angels' or two camps of angels flanking him, and adds that Mahanaim lay in Gad and became a town of consequence.

Henry reports the rabbinic account that one host was the guardian angels of Mesopotamia delivering him to the angels of Canaan, but prefers two hosts set before and behind, guarding him from Laban at his back and Esau in his face. Calvin reports the Hebrew interpreters differently, as placing the enemy's camp on one side and God on the other, judges it likelier that the angels stood on both sides so that Jacob might see himself everywhere fortified, and is content also to take the dual for a plural. Keil and Delitzsch pass straight from the naming to the embassy, making Mahanaim the point from which Jacob opens communication with Esau. Henry presses the comfort, that a good man may see by faith what Jacob saw with his eyes, and that there is no need to dispute whether each saint has a guardian angel when he has a guard of them, which Wesley repeats almost word for word. Calvin makes the same observation a rebuke, that those who allow each man only one angel depreciate God's kindness, while Clarke turns it against the invocation of angels under feigned names, since they are instruments without discretionary power, whose own word is that we should worship God.
3:
Gill and Clarke note that the word for messengers is the one rendered angels two verses before, though Gill denies Jarchi's inference that they were angels. Clarke thinks the embassy was sent before the vision at Mahanaim, the messengers returning only at the Jabbok. Henry observes that Jacob's road did not require him to pass through Esau's country but lay near it, and he would not go by without the respect due to an only brother, an elder brother, and a brother offended. Henry and Wesley read the titles as a disclaimer, Jacob calling Esau lord and himself servant to signify that he did not insist on the prerogatives of birthright and blessing.

Calvin states the difficulty, that Jacob seems to cede the dominion he had contended for at the hazard of his life, so that the hatred, the danger and the twenty years of banishment went for nothing. His answer is that Jacob gives up the temporal dominion while yielding nothing of his right to the secret benediction, content with the hope of an inheritance yet concealed. On the oxen and asses Calvin denies any boasting, holding that Jacob names his wealth to incline Esau to humanity and to remove the fear of expense. Ellicott reads the enumeration the same way, as showing that Jacob claimed no share of Isaac's property, Wesley that he came neither as fugitive nor beggar.

Ellicott reconstructs the situation, news having reached Jacob of Esau at the head of a body of retainers on an expedition against the Horites, a cave-dwelling people unable to cope with him. Esau's home was still at Hebron, and the raid revealed both the weakness of the inhabitants and a country suited to hunting, so that he removed there when his father died. Clarke places Seir south of the Dead Sea as far as the Arabian gulf, taken from the Horites by Esau, in which he finds the prediction verified that he should live by his sword. Calvin sees providence in the removal, the land of promise being left vacant without slaughter among brethren, and conjectures that Esau, grown rich and impatient of remaining a child in his father's house, chose a barren country he could name after himself.

Calvin adds that Malachi calls it a banishment, so that Esau, departing willingly, was by secret counsel deprived of the land he coveted. Clarke takes the four hundred men for no evidence of hostility, judging that Esau came to do his brother honour, and lays Jacob's alarm to a guilty conscience, with Horace's tag that a clear conscience is a wall of brass. Calvin agrees that Esau advanced with benevolence and the fear had no cause, but sees a purpose in it, that God suffers us to dread things not terrible in themselves lest faith grow torpid. He warns that those who fancy faith exempt from fear have never known what faith is, God promising not to remove the sense of danger but to keep fear from overwhelming us.

Gill judges the alarm a plain failure of faith, after so many promises and an appearance of angels given as his guard. Ellicott says the same more mildly, the distress showing a faith feeble but real, since it drove him to prayer; Henry defends him, holding that a lively apprehension of danger may consist with humble confidence in God's promise, as Christ in his agony was amazed. Henry reads the division of the company as for flight and not, like Abraham's, for fight. Clarke calls it prudence turned at last into a right channel, and Calvin observes that panic deprives men of discretion, so that a plan this deliberate proceeded from faith; the word for the two bands, he adds, is the word for the host of angels behind Mahanaim. Keil and Delitzsch join the two bands to the prayer that follows, fear driving Jacob to the Helper.
9:
Ellicott calls this the first prayer recorded in Scripture, remarkable for joining earnestness to simplicity, Jacob addressing God first as the God of his fathers and then as the Jehovah who had commanded the return. Clarke treats it as a model in five parts, self-abasement, the magnifying of mercy, deprecation of the evil feared, the pleading of promises, and encouragement from what God had done. Henry observes that whatever frightens us should drive us to our knees, and that Jacob, lately shown his guard of angels, applied not to them but to God. Calvin finds in the prayer proof that fear had not prevented faith from proving victorious, Jacob casting his cares into his Father's bosom without hesitation.

Henry and Wesley note that he does not call God his own but a God in covenant with his ancestors, and could plead that covenant the better because it was entailed on him. Calvin explains the titles differently, that since men cannot ascend to God's throne he comes down, and by calling himself the God of Abraham and Isaac invites their son. Calvin finds Jacob supported as by two pillars, the command and the promise, since the rule of prayer is sought in God's word and whoever relies on neither casts empty words in the air. He calls it holy boldness to ask familiarly for what God has promised, and infers that Jacob cannot have lied to his wives about the command to return.

Henry calls the plea of unworthiness surprising, since Jacob might have urged that what was in danger was his own and dearly earned; Christ, he notes, commended most those who called themselves unworthy. Gill and Clarke prefer the marginal rendering, that he is less than all the mercies shown him, Clarke comparing Paul's less than the least of all saints. Calvin sets the confession against Satan's craft, which would keep us from praying by asking who we are that we should enter God's presence. Jacob anticipates it, Calvin says, by owning himself unworthy of the former gifts, so that their magnitude breeds no distrust but assures him God will be what he has been.

Henry and Wesley take the staff to mean he crossed poor and desolate, without guide or attendant, and Clarke says the Chaldee rightly renders it himself alone. Both note that though distress had obliged the dividing into two bands, Jacob turns it into a measure of his increase, since those whose latter end is greatly increased should remember their small beginning. Henry turns it into a plea, that God who kept him with one staff will keep him now that so many are embarked with him. Calvin observes that Jacob comprises the mercies under one head, the antithesis between his former solitude and his present affluence, and that mercy paired with truth teaches that good flows from free favour.

Henry notes that the request is single and express, that we may be particular with God, and that the fear which quickens prayer is itself pleadable. On the mother with the children Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin agree that the words are proverbial for unsparing cruelty, taken from the bird that covers its young, Calvin picturing a hawk emptying the nest. Ellicott dwells on the same image, Jacob's mind resting not on his own death but on the mother slain upon her offspring, while Clarke infers what an awful opinion Jacob held of his brother. Henry draws the rule that the best we can say to God is what he has said to us, Jacob asking what becomes of the promised multitude if they are all cut off. Clarke observes that he stopped there, his faith confirmed by the promise that ratified the covenant to Abraham and Isaac; Ellicott adds that though among men recalling a promise may be ungenerous, with God each act of mercy pledges more.
13:
Henry frames the section as the complement of the prayer, Jacob having made God his friend now making Esau his friend, since his fear did not sink into the despair that dispirits from using means, nor his prayer presume on mercy without them. Calvin says the same at more length, warning that men commonly contrive vain subterfuges after praying, yet that security must not make us indolent, since the Lord will have his aids applied to use. He distinguishes the diligence of the pious from the world's restless activity, which, relying on its own industry, neither asks what is lawful nor escapes trepidation. Keil and Delitzsch put it briefly, that hoping for safety from the Lord alone Jacob neglected no means, and Ellicott judges that faith had regained the ascendancy in a man who put everything into Esau's power.

Clarke calls it a princely present, enough to compensate Esau for the loss of birthright and blessing, and dwells on the milch camels as a principal part of Arab wealth, quoting Pliny on their milk mixed with three parts water. He prefers ten bulls to the twenty of the Syriac and Vulgate as the right proportion to forty kine, and reads the whole transaction as restitution. Calvin measures the gift against the promise, since a man enriched by his own labour is proportionally tenacious, and Jacob might have found some quiet nook and kept his property entire, yet purchases at this price a peaceable abode in Canaan. Few follow God, he adds, because scarcely one in a hundred will bear to be a loser. Henry counts the beasts at five hundred and eighty where Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott make them five hundred and fifty, and finds in them evidence of God's blessing and of Jacob's wisdom in parting with some to secure the rest.

Keil and Delitzsch note that the selection matches what nomads held, as in Job, and that the proportion of males to females follows Varro's rule for husbandry. On the spaces between the droves they, Calvin and Ellicott agree that the object was to mitigate Esau's anger by degrees, Ellicott adding that the Hebrew word is a breathing place. Henry and Wesley report the message the drovers were to carry, calling Esau their lord and Jacob his servant, and above all saying that Jacob was coming behind lest he suspect a flight; Gill explains that the present would have counted for nothing without the visit. Ellicott takes I will appease him literally, that Jacob will cover his brother's face with the offering and afterwards see it, and notes that covering the face of the offended party became the standing legal term for atonement.

Clarke glosses what came to his hand as what providence had put in his power, while Ellicott reports the Jewish reading of precious stones and argues that it means what he had with him, implying no selection. Clarke says the Jabbok rises in the mountains of Gilead and falls into the Jordan, and Ellicott identifies it with the Wady Zerka, afterwards the border between Manasseh and Gad, running in a ravine so rapid that Tristram found the water at his horse's girths. Calvin gives the same modern name, places the stream on the northern border of the Ammonites, and observes that it is alluded to in the wrestling that follows and so given here by anticipation. Ellicott argues from the width of the ravine that the brook means the valley rather than the stream, so that Jacob saw his people to the high ground beyond and stayed on the south side, which he thinks proved by Peniel's lying in Gad. Calvin says he stayed not to escape if he heard of their destruction but because solitude suited prayer, and draws a threefold order: resort first to the Lord, then use what means offer, then go forward without dread.
24:
Keil and Delitzsch place Jacob alone on the northern side of the Jabbok, and derive the verb for wrestling, which occurs nowhere else, from a root meaning to plant limb against limb, the river being named from the struggle. Ellicott agrees that the word was chosen for its likeness to Jabbok but derives it, with Calvin citing Gesenius, from a word for dust. Henry leaves the wrestler's identity open between a created angel and the eternal Word, being sure only that God's name was in him. Gill calls him the Son of God in the form of man, and Clarke asserts that it was the Lord Jesus Christ, styled an angel as the messenger of the great counsel.

Clarke argues that the body was appearance only, since an angel can raise in the imagination every idea of corporeity without substance, and bodies really assumed could not vanish in a moment. Ellicott denies the premise from the other side, holding that there is no warrant for making the angel an incarnation of Deity, any more than with Manoah, but a mediate manifestation pointing to the coming of the Word in flesh. He also rejects the reading of the narrative as allegory, contradicted by the change of name and the lameness. Calvin insists that neither Satan nor a mortal wrestled with Jacob but God himself, Moses calling him a man because he appeared under that form.

On Calvin's reading the vision makes every servant of God a wrestler, God being the author of our crosses and descending into the arena himself to try our strength. He states the objection, that to contend with one at whose breath all flesh perishes were insane temerity, and answers that we fight only by his own power, he assailing with one hand and defending with the other. Raw recruits are spared and young oxen not yoked at once, he adds, so Jacob is now led out to real war. The lesson is that Jacob was warned at the border of the promised land not to expect a tranquil life there, since we dream of a truce in perpetual war unless the Lord rouse us.

Henry calls it a single combat hand to hand, God himself seeming to dispute the pass, and notes from Hosea that Jacob's weapons were prayers and tears, the wrestling being spiritual as well as bodily, as Clarke also draws from that prophet. Henry and Wesley explain that the angel prevailed not, meaning the discouragement neither shook Jacob's faith nor silenced his prayer, and that he wrestled in strength derived from heaven. Gill puts it that he prevailed not because he would not, and that the promises and Jacob's pleading of them left him no other course.

Clarke doubts a complete dislocation, since the Hebrew often means to smite with violence and a blow to the groin would disable without danger; Ellicott takes the hollow for the socket and the verb for a sprain. Henry and Wesley think Jacob felt little pain, since he did not halt till the struggle was over, and call it a divine touch that wounded and healed at once, believers winning victories and still coming off with broken bones. Calvin makes the wound the point, the mark lasting all Jacob's days so that the vision might not seem a dream, and the faithful conquering only by being injured. Ellicott renders the parting words send me away, for the gleam of morning has gone up, and takes the request for an acknowledgement of defeat, so that Jacob asks a blessing as his ransom. Clarke thinks the daybreak meant only that Jacob must rejoin his family, most angelic appearances having happened in open day; Calvin adds that daylight would have brought witnesses to a vision meant for Jacob alone, and Henry finds in the request a condescension honouring a faith that would rather be dislocated than go away unblessed.
27:
Wesley states the exchange plainly, that Jacob confessed himself a supplanter and was told he should be so called no more but Israel, a prince with God, adding that one who has prevailed for a blessing from heaven will not fail of Esau's favour. Keil and Delitzsch render the name God's fighter, while Clarke allows both a derivation from the word for prince and another from the words for man and seeing, answering to the name Jacob gave the place. Clarke prefers a literal rendering of the last clause, thou hast had power with God and with man thou shalt also prevail, finding a deliberate opposition between the strong God and weak man. Calvin follows Jerome to the same effect, and adds that the old name is not abolished, being itself a token of grace, and that God gives with a name the thing it implies.

Ellicott takes Israel to mean a prince of God, observes that Esau had put a bad sense on the name Jacob and not undeservedly, and finds the new name matched by a changed character, the crafty schemer becoming humble and penitent. Gill explains the request for the wrestler's name as emboldened by the gift of a new one, and thinks Jacob knew him already for God but hoped for a title drawn from the place, as God elsewhere is called the God of Bethel. Clarke suspects a more dangerous motive, that Jacob wanted a name by which to invoke him, which might have bred idolatry; Ellicott compares the like refusal to Manoah. Calvin raises the difficulty that Jacob had already acknowledged him as God in asking his blessing, and answers that he wished to ascend beyond an obscure knowledge, a desire not granted because the fathers walked in twilight until Christ arose.

Gill and Ellicott note that the place is called Penuel in the next verse and probably should be read so here, Gill adding that a city was afterwards built there. Calvin commends Jacob's care that the memory of the grace should not perish, the vision concerning not him alone but the whole Church, and dwells on the thanksgiving for being snatched from death, since God's glory would destroy us unsustained. Gill and Clarke read the rising sun as an emblem of the Sun of righteousness with healing in his wings, Clarke asking whether Malachi had this passage in view and suggesting that the pain passed with the dawn. Ellicott takes the opposite view, that Jacob did not discover his lameness until he tried to walk, the injury declaring itself as the sinews cooled; Calvin thinks the halting painless so that the miracle might be plainer, and Wesley reports the opinion that he limped to his grave.

On the sinew Ellicott allows that the received rendering has authority, the Greek having the sinew that became numb and the Vulgate the sinew that withered, but prefers the proper name of the great tendon running down the thigh, which Keil and Delitzsch identify as the nerve most easily injured in wrestling. Ellicott adds the Jewish observation that this was the second ordinance laid on Abraham's race after circumcision, and grew out of an event in their forefather's life, to whose reality it bears witness. Clarke declines the question, since neither Jew nor Christian can tell what sinew is meant, though on his reading of the injury it must be sought in the groin. Gill calls the abstinence very superstitious and cites the Mishnah, which forbids the sinew within the land and without, in common food and in sacrifices alike. Calvin denies the charge, holding it not superstition but the discipline of a Church in its infancy, and reports that the Jews of his day, no longer knowing which sinew or even which thigh was meant, abstained from both hind quarters and sold those parts to Christians.
